final_recommendation: The room converged on a protocol amendment with binding Article 4 language: monthly joint inspections, unrestricted union access, automatic tariff suspension at day 120, labor-only scope. Democratic caucus commits to floor vote the week after December 15th signature.
minority_objections: Mexico initially resisted 90-day timeline and U.S.-only inspectors, demanding joint teams and 120 days to preserve sovereignty
Canada insisted amendment remain strictly labor-focused with zero changes to dairy, Chapter 19, or market access
key_conflicts: Timeline tension: Democrats demanded 90-day remedy window; Mexico countered with 120 days to avoid 'punishment before remedy'
Inspection authority: Labor unions demanded independent inspectors; Mexico required joint Mexican-American teams to preserve sovereignty
Announcement timing: Labor demanded Friday public release to maintain base momentum; others needed locked text first
key_concessions: Democrats accepted 120-day timeline (from initial 90-day demand) in exchange for automatic tariff triggers
Mexico accepted binding monthly inspections and unrestricted union access in exchange for joint inspection teams (no U.S. auditors alone)
Business lobby accepted amendment uncertainty in exchange for firm December 15th signature and floor vote timeline
All parties accepted labor-only amendment scope to preserve Canada's settled terms
red_lines: Democrats: Article 4 must say Mexico 'shall' conduct inspections (not 'endeavor to'), no side letters, binding text only
Mexico: Joint inspection teams only, no U.S. auditors operating alone in Mexican plants
Canada: Amendment strictly labor verification/enforcement—zero changes to dairy tariffs, Chapter 19, or market access
Labor unions: Automatic tariff suspension with no Mexico veto or renegotiation window
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Mexican Congressional ratification risk: Mexico's domestic politics barely surfaced despite sovereignty concerns
Implementation capacity: No discussion of whether Mexico can operationally deliver monthly inspections across all facilities
Business disruption during 120-day remedy window: Tariff suspension impact on supply chains not explored
Public interpretation risk: Whether 'joint teams' will be read as weakening enforcement or strengthening sovereignty
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Article 4 binding language actually prevents Mexican deferrals in practice
Whether joint inspection teams can move fast enough to meet 120-day remedy deadlines
Whether Friday announcement generates sufficient labor base mobilization before December 15th
Whether Canadian Parliament accepts labor-only scope as credible constraint on future amendments
Whether Mexican Congress ratifies protocol amendment given sovereignty concerns
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved convergence on protocol amendment structure and timeline but left unresolved: (1) operational feasibility of monthly inspections across Mexico's manufacturing base, (2) whether 'joint teams' will satisfy both labor's enforcement demands and Mexico's sovereignty requirements in practice, (3) Mexican Congressional ratification pathway given elevated sovereignty concerns, (4) whether the Friday announcement narrative will successfully frame joint teams as enforcement-with-teeth rather than enforcement-with-compromise.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Democrats opened with 'votes aren't there as written' and repeatedly demanded binding text before floor vote; ratification contingency drove every negotiation round
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Labor unions set hard requirements (independent inspectors, wage audits, no delays) and threatened to walk if Article 4 wasn't mandatory; drove shift from text-only to binding enforcement mechanism
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business conditioned support on firm timeline and no reopening, but accepted amendment uncertainty; present but not dominant—scored medium because it shaped constraints rather than driving outcomes
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada repeatedly demanded labor-only scope to avoid defending dairy concessions, secured explicit language in announcement; genuine constraint but not the room's central driver
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexico's insistence on joint teams (not U.S. auditors alone) shaped every enforcement proposal; sovereignty concerns spiked with binding Article 4 and drove the 120-day compromise
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media actor pushed for Friday announcement and enforcement-with-teeth narrative to maintain base momentum; influenced timing and framing but didn't drive substantive terms
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Room treated amendment as necessary to achieve ratification—'this dies in Ways and Means' without protocol fix; stability explicitly contingent on domestic-ratification compromise throughout
